"Aft" means toward the back of a vessel — a ship, a boat, a submarine, or an aircraft. That single idea is the heart of this word.

To understand "aft," you first need to know that every vessel has two ends:

  • The front end is called the bow (or the fore).
  • The back end is called the stern.

"Aft" always points to the stern — the rear end of the vessel.
How It Works as an Adverb

As an adverb, "aft" answers the question "Where?" or "In which direction?" It tells you where something is located or where someone is moving — toward the back.

Look at these examples:

  • "The sailor walked aft."
    → The sailor walked toward the back of the ship.
  • "The engine is mounted aft."
    → The engine is placed at the back of the ship.
  • "Move aft immediately!"
    → Move toward the rear right now!

Notice that "aft" is not describing a person or a thing — it is describing where the action is happening. That is exactly the job of an adverb.

The opposite of "aft" is "fore" (sometimes "forward"), which means toward the front of the vessel.

  • "The anchor is stored fore." → at the front.
  • "The lifeboats are kept aft." → at the back.

You will encounter "aft" most often in the phrase "fore and aft," which means from the very front all the way to the very back — the entire length of the vessel, with nothing left out.

  • "The captain searched the ship fore and aft."
    → The captain searched the entire ship, from the front end to the back end. No corner was skipped.

This phrase carries a sense of thoroughness and completeness. Over time, it has also been borrowed into general English to mean "from one end to the other" even outside of ships.
A Critical Boundary: Where "Aft" Does NOT Belong

"Aft" is not a general word for "behind" or "at the back." It is tied specifically to vessels and aircraft. You would never say:

  • ❌ "The kitchen is aft of the living room."
  • ❌ "She sat aft of him in the classroom."

These are wrong. In everyday life, away from ships and planes, you simply use "behind" or "at the back." "Aft" lives in nautical and aviation contexts — and that is where it stays.

Sailors coined "aft," but pilots and flight crews borrowed it. If a flight attendant says "Please move aft," they mean: move toward the back of the aircraft. The same meaning, the same logic — just in the air instead of on the water.
The Full Picture in One Sentence

"Aft" as an adverb means: at, toward, or in the direction of the rear end of a ship or aircraft — and it describes where something is or where movement is headed.

Everything else — "fore and aft," its contrast with "fore," its aviation use — is simply this one core meaning applied in different situations.
